earlyEstimate.title: Early yield estimate: honest backtest
earlyEstimate.tagline: How well the nowcast predicts a season's yield before the survey is published, compared plainly against two naive guesses.
earlyEstimate.empty: No backtest data for this crop and season.
earlyEstimate.leadCaption: Mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) across every held-out year, leave-one-year-out. Lower is better. The best model for this lead time is bolded.
earlyEstimate.yearsNote: Based on {{n}} held-out years of leave-one-year-out cross-validation.
earlyEstimate.honestyTitle: Why this page shows every model, not just the best one
earlyEstimate.honestyBody1: A model that always beat the naive guess would be worth building UI around on its own. That is often not what the numbers show here: for several crops, simply predicting a district's own historical average is the best or tied-best model at every lead time. This page shows all four candidates side by side, for every crop and lead time, rather than only the winner, so the real gap between "a model exists" and "a model helps" stays visible.
earlyEstimate.honestyBody2: Where a fancier model does win, the margin is checked against how much the result swings from year to year: an improvement smaller than that year-to-year spread is not treated as a real edge. See the methodology page for how each figure is computed.

scenario.title: Scenario explorer
scenario.tagline: Model-based estimates of mean yield under different combinations of farming practices, for one district, crop and season at a time.
scenario.pickCaption: Toggle practices to see this district's precomputed estimate for that exact combination.
scenario.pickEmpty: No precomputed scenario for this district and crop.
scenario.allCombosCaption: Every combination of the 4 levers below, sorted by predicted mean yield. Your current selection above is highlighted.
scenario.disclaimerTitle: What this is, and what it is not
scenario.disclaimerBody: Every number on this page is a precomputed, model-based estimate from the driver model (LightGBM + SHAP), read off a fixed grid of 16 lever combinations per district and crop. It is not a live simulation, not a policy guarantee, and not a causal claim: it shows what the model associates with a given combination of practices in plots that already look like that, not what would happen if a specific farmer adopted them.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.tagline: How every number on this site is computed, in plain language, with the honest limitations included.
methodology.yieldBody: Yield (kg per hectare) is computed only from pure-stand plots (one main crop on the plot) farmed by small-scale farmers, using each plot's harvested weight divided by its area, and combined into a district figure with the Seasonal Agricultural Survey's own sampling weights, strata and clusters. The yield gap is the modeled attainable yield minus this actual yield, shown in kg/ha and as a percent of attainable.
methodology.attainableBody1: Attainable yield is the survey-weighted 90th percentile of yield already achieved on comparable plots: what the best-performing tenth of farmers in a similar zone, crop and season already do, not a theoretical agronomic maximum.
methodology.attainableBody2: "Comparable" plots are grouped into 5 zones by a k-means clustering of district-level soil and cropland features, because no agro-ecological zone map is available for this project. This is a documented stand-in, not an authoritative zone boundary.
methodology.driversBody1: For each crop, a LightGBM model is trained to relate practices (improved seed, fertilizer, irrigation, erosion control, and more) and plot conditions to yield, and explained with SHAP to rank which factors go together with higher or lower yield. This model is validated by holding out entire districts, never a random split, since plots in the same district are not independent.
methodology.driversBody2: These rankings are associations only. A practice appearing alongside higher yield does not mean adopting it would cause that yield: farmers who adopt one good practice often adopt several, and better land can attract both investment and naturally higher yield. One crop's model (sorghum) does not currently beat a simple naive baseline; its rankings are shown anyway, plainly labeled, rather than hidden.
methodology.nowcastBody1: Before a season's survey results are published, satellite vegetation (MODIS NDVI) and rainfall (CHIRPS) measured partway through the season, plus the district's own recent yield history, are used to estimate that season's yield. Every prediction is checked with leave-one-year-out cross-validation against two naive guesses: the district's own historical average, and last year's same-season figure.
methodology.nowcastBody2: The honest result, shown in full on the early estimate page, is that the naive historical-average guess is the best or tied-best model for most crops and lead times. This is reported directly rather than presented as a working forecast where the evidence does not support that.
methodology.scenarioBody: The scenario explorer looks up a precomputed table (16 combinations of 4 practices, per district and crop) built from the driver model's own fitted associations, with a bootstrapped interval. It is a lookup, not a live simulation, and never claims to predict the effect of a real policy change.
methodology.reliabilityBody1: Every number on this site carries a confidence interval, a reliability flag, or both. A cell is flagged based on how many survey clusters (segments) and plots back it:
methodology.reliabilityOk: Ok: enough surveyed plots and clusters for a reasonably precise estimate.
methodology.reliabilityCaution: Use with caution: meets the minimum cluster count, but the estimate's variability is elevated.
methodology.reliabilitySuppressed: Suppressed: too few surveyed clusters to report responsibly. The cell is shown greyed out, not hidden, per this project's own transparency rule.
methodology.validationBody: As a credibility check, this project's own national maize yield estimate for Season B 2025 (1,400 kg/ha) was compared against NISR's own published figure for the same period (1,300 kg/ha): a 7.7% difference, well inside this project's own 95% confidence interval. Area and production totals diverge more, by design, since this project's estimate covers pure-stand plots only while NISR's published totals include intercropped plots too.

data.title: Data sources
data.tagline: Every dataset behind this site, and what it is used for.
data.surveyCaption: The primary source for all yield, practice, and gap figures.
data.surveyBody: Seasonal Agricultural Survey microdata, 2019 to 2025, Seasons A and B, National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR). Raw survey microdata is never published or shown here; only district-level, survey-weighted aggregates with a minimum sample size appear on this site.
data.satelliteCaption: Used for the early yield estimate and the driver model's soil and rainfall features, via Google Earth Engine.

satelliteUse.ndvi: vegetation greenness signal for the early estimate
satelliteUse.rainfall: rainfall totals and anomalies for the early estimate and driver model
satelliteUse.cropland: masks NDVI and rainfall to cropland pixels only
satelliteUse.soil: soil pH, nitrogen, carbon and texture features for the driver model
satelliteUse.terrain: elevation context for zoning and features

data.privacyBody: No individual farmer, household, or plot-level data ever leaves the processing pipeline or reaches this site. Every figure shown here is aggregated to at least the district x crop x season x year level, with a minimum sample size before it is shown at all.

about.title: About AgriTwin Rwanda
about.tagline: Yield gap and early harvest estimation for Rwanda, built for the NISR 2026 Big Data Hackathon.
about.projectBody1: Rwanda's Seasonal Agricultural Survey measures land use, crop area, inputs and production every season, but results are only published after the season ends. AgriTwin Rwanda combines that survey data with satellite and climate data to show, for each district and crop, how far actual yield falls below what similar farmers already achieve nearby, what practices are associated with that gap, and an early, honestly-validated estimate of how the season is shaping up before the official numbers arrive.
about.projectBody2: Built for Track 1 (Agricultural Productivity) of the NISR 2026 Big Data Hackathon, aligned with Rwanda's NST2 priorities and Vision 2050 goals around agricultural productivity and climate resilience.
about.teamBody: A two-person team: one member covering data engineering, the API and the web app, and one covering survey methodology, validation, Kinyarwanda review, and domain research.
about.aiBody: This project used AI coding assistance throughout its build. Every AI-assisted session is logged in the project's public AI usage log with what was built and what a human reviewed. The Kinyarwanda translations on this site are an AI-authored first draft, not yet reviewed by a native speaker.
about.contactBody: The full source code, methodology notes, and decision log for this project are available in its repository, alongside a documentation site covering the data pipeline, models, and API in more detail.
